Referral Note (primary care)

Ms. Lawson, a 42-year-old middle school teacher, is referred for psychiatric evaluation. For more than two years she has returned repeatedly with a range of health concerns, most recently occasional mild headaches, muscle aches, and fatigue. Over the past year her workup has included multiple CT scans, colonoscopy, upper endoscopy, cardiac evaluation, mammography, and laboratory studies, all unremarkable. She frequently searches medical information online and schedules appointments with specialists whenever she notices minor physical sensations. She remains concerned that a serious illness is being missed and has been missing work for medical appointments. Medical history is notable for hypertension, managed with lisinopril. No previous psychiatric treatment. Referred for evaluation and treatment recommendations.

Behavioral Observations (on arrival)

Appearance: Appropriately groomed.

Behavior: Alert and cooperative. Mildly anxious throughout the interview. Brought a folder of her prior test results to the visit.

Speech: Normal.

Mood / Affect: Mood "worried." Affect anxious but appropriate.

Thought / Perception: Thought processes logical. Thought content demonstrates persistent illness preoccupation without delusions.

Cognition / Insight: Insight limited; judgment intact.

These are the four questions of your seven-minute oral defense. When the defense begins, face your camera and present in one continuous recording, as though presenting to your collaborating psychiatrist or interdisciplinary treatment team.
1. State your primary DSM-5-TR diagnosis and ICD-10-CM diagnosis code.
Explain why this diagnosis best fits the patient's presentation by discussing at least three to four specific clinical findings from the case.
2. Discuss the single most important differential diagnosis.
Explain why this diagnosis was considered and why it was ruled out using evidence from the patient presentation.
3. Present your initial evidence-based treatment recommendations.
Discuss:
  • Appropriate level of care
  • Medication recommendation (or explain why medication is not indicated)
  • Appropriate psychotherapy
  • One patient education point or safety consideration
4. Conclude your presentation by answering the following question.
What additional question, assessment, or diagnostic information would you obtain before finalizing your diagnosis or treatment plan, and why is this information clinically important?
